utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, ladies and gentlemen; good morning, technicians; good morning, interpreters. I can see that they are there. Good morning to our assistants, representatives of the Registrar. Good morning, counsel for the Prosecution, counsel for Defence. Good morning, General Krstic. Good morning, Witness J. Have you had a good rest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you have a nice weekend here in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it was good. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just remind you, Witness, that you are still under oath, and you will continue answering questions that will be put to you by Mr. Cayley, whom you know already. Mr. Cayley, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness J.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Witness J, I'm just going to refresh your memory as to where we were on Friday and what you said to the Judges --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: -- so that I can give you the point in time which we reached in your testimony. Now, you explained to the Judges that on the 12th of July of 1995 you found yourself in a meadow, in a place called Lolici. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we were not there on the 12th, we were in Lolici on the 13th. And on the 12th we were still in Jaglici.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, you're quite right, Witness. Thank you for correcting me. And I think you explained to the Judges that the Bosnian Serb soldiers searched you for money; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And I think you also said to the Judges that you heard someone whisper in front of you that there were about 2.000 Muslim men on the meadow; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think we got to a point in time when you explained that water was brought to you and a man in front of you complained that he had not had any water, and then a soldier beat him and then shot him.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and he killed him. The soldier killed the civilian who had asked for water. He said that somebody had had water two times already and that he hadn't had any water so far, so two soldiers kicked him; one kicked him on the left side of his head, the other on the right side, and he started bleeding from his mouth. So one of them then grabbed him by the neck and the other took him as well, and they dragged him away some six metres and they shot him, and he remained there, lying dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, I think the next thing that happened to you is some Bosnian Serb soldiers recognised a Muslim police officer amongst you; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that. They recognised a policeman who was a neighbour of mine, who used to work in Vlasenica during peacetime. So they pointed their finger at him and one of them called him out. He addressed him by his last name and he told him, "Come here." So he came up and five or six soldiers gathered around him, they said hello to him, all of them, and I was glad to see that because I thought, well, here's someone who knows us, so they might help us. But they took him away to a house that was situated on the left-hand side, and they stayed there for about one hour, one hour and a half, and after that, three of them came back with him. And they stood next to us, on the left side, and he called his brother and he said, "Give me your jacket," so he did and they asked him, "Who is this guy here?" and he said, "This is my brother." And then he turned around and he called his second brother. So they left again, they went in the right direction, towards the house where the wounded were, and I don't know what happened to them. I didn't hear shots but I never saw them again.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Witness, these three men, they were taken away by Bosnian Serb soldiers.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the soldiers, and ever since then we haven't heard of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Excuse me. He said they were taken to the house where the wounded were. Who was wounded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Above the house, behind the house where the wounded were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: There were wounded people behind the house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: The wounded were in the house, and the three brothers were taken above the house, to the right-hand side, and I haven't heard of them ever since.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness, were there Muslim wounded in the house to which the three brothers were taken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were wounded in the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour Judge Riad, does that answer your question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Witness, there was a road that ran in front of the meadow where you were sitting. Do you recall --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, an asphalt road.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you recall at any time seeing buses or trucks on that road?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both buses and trucks were passing and they were travelling from Potocari towards Milici. They were transporting civilians from Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you see the people on those buses and trucks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were people, including women and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you recognise them as your people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't recognise anyone. I wasn't really watching. I kept my head down because I kept thinking only about my fate.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, while you were in Lolici, I think the Bosnian Serb soldiers asked for 30 volunteers from the men. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that. They came to us and they said that they needed about 30 young men, aged approximately 25. So 30 of them came out and they boarded a truck. They gave them some shovels and the truck left. I don't know what happened to them. I don't know where they were taken, but any trace of them was lost.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think there came a time when a VRS officer came to the meadow, do you remember that, and gave assurances that everything would be all right.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: First they searched us, looking for money, asking for money. And there was one person whom they addressed as Madzarevic, and Madzarevic -- people were from Visnjica. One of them had blonde hair and a ponytail, and he had some kind of black bandanna on his head. So they searched us and they took six marks from me and -- 600 marks and some necklaces that belonged to my daughter. And then Mladic came and he spoke to us. The first thing he said was, "Isn't this better than to get killed? Naser has abandoned you. He fled to Tuzla. It is not a very good idea to wage war with Serbs. We have almost evacuated all of our families and they have been put up in Tuzla, Kladanj, and Zivinice, and most probably within a day or two you will be exchanged as well. Everyone will find his family. Nobody is going to beat you. Nobody is going to provoke you. You will be given food and you're very hot here so we will find you some shade." So everybody applauded, saying "Thank you, sir. Thank you, General." He kind of encouraged us. But I wanted to speak to him and he said, "What's the problem?" I said, "General, you see I'm barefoot, I've lost my boots. I have a pair of shoes in my backpack. Can I go and get them?" And then he told me, "You will get a pair of shoes." And then I said, "Thank you, General." And then he left. Then 15 -- 20 minutes later, the one who was wearing a civilian uniform, without any insignia, he said -- he told us to make a column by four. So the one who had given this order was a few metres away from us.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If I could interrupt you just to clarify one thing. Did Mladic say to you that your families had been evacuated to Tuzla, Kladanj, and Zivinice?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you then said 30 minutes later you were instructed to --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between 20 and 30 minutes later.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: -- you were instructed to make a column for 4 by 4. Can you tell the Judges once you formed that column where you went?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know the area. When I -- after I had come out with the person who had been with me in the warehouse, he told me that we were somewhere near Kravica. They brought us to a warehouse and both sides of the column, there would be a Serb soldiers every six metres armed with automatic rifles. They had ammunition belts across their chests, and they were marching us a warehouse where a bus was parked just outside the warehouse. And I entered the warehouse through the second door, not the first one. So the warehouse was completely full, and I found a seat in one of the corners of the warehouse. And the soldier who was standing at the right side of the warehouse, he cursed at me and he told me to sit down. And I told him that I wanted to stand, to lean against the wall because I had back pain. And this is how I sat down in that warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness, before we move to the next part of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 8/4, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The column of men that you described to the Judges, do you recall how long that column was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my estimate, because I could see it when we turned around the curve, I was somewhere in the middle of the column. I think that the column was between 400 and 500 metres long. I couldn't tell the exact number, but this is according to my estimate. Because we were all terrified. We didn't know what was going to happen to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I understand that, Witness. When you entered the warehouse, how full was it with Muslim men. Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: The warehouse was completely full. If you had thrown a lighter or a match inside, it would have stayed on somebody's shoulder or in somebody's lap, it couldn't have fallen on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, if you could first of all put the photograph in front of the witness and let the witness look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I've shown you this photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first door, the first entrance and this is the second one [indicates]. And this is where I entered through the second one, and this is where I got out, through this door. The truck, the excavator was there when I got out the night between Thursday and Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness, if you could stop for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And Mr. Usher, if you could place the photograph on to the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness, what I want you to do now, I don't want you to speak, I just want you to point to the door in the warehouse through which you entered, and you can use the pointer.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, if you could give the witness the pointer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is through this door that I entered [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness, you'll need to point on the photograph. Can you see which door?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: This door here [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you could keep the pointer on that door.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, if you could help the witness. Let the record show that the witness is indicating a small door on the right-hand side of the photograph. It's a small door with some writing above it and it's the last door on the extreme right hand of the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And that's the warehouse, is it, Witness, which you entered?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness, if you could explain to the Judges what you recall happened next?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the warehouse, when we got in, when the last person entered through the same door where I had entered, he didn't have a place to sit down, so he remained standing. And he was kicked by a Serb soldier in the back. And the soldier told him -- he cursed at him and he told him to sit down. And this man turned around and he said, "I have no room to sit down." And then there was a burst of gunfire that mowed him down. And all of a sudden there was a lot of shooting in the warehouse, and we didn't know where it was coming from. There were rifles, grenades, bursts of gunfire and it was -- it got so dark in the warehouse that we couldn't see anything. People started to scream, to shout, crying for help. And then there would be a lull, and then all of a sudden it would start again. And they kept shooting like that until nightfall in the warehouse. I managed to reach an outside gate, a little booth, and I found a neighbour of mine there, and he told me to lie down. And I asked him if he was wounded and he wasn't, and he asked me if I was wounded and I wasn't either. And there was blood underneath and I couldn't take it any longer. I pulled a dead body over me, and this is how I remained for about 24 hours in the warehouse. In the next morning, one could tell that it was dawning. This neighbour of mine stood up, and he said that he needed to urinate because he was thirsty, he couldn't take it anymore. So I grabbed him -- pulled him by his coat and told him to lie down but then there was a burst of gunfire and he fell down. So I spent the whole day of the 14th of July in the warehouse. I didn't know what time of day it was. Somebody asked us at one point if there was anyone healthy amongst us to join their army. So a couple of people went out but I didn't watch. So I don't know who left. And there was a sound of a truck that left, but I don't know in which direction it left. All of a sudden, I could hear a voice crying, "Salko, Salko," for about 15 times. And then somebody cursed us about our Turkish mothers. And then we heard a voice, "Is there anybody alive amongst you?" And then we heard a shoot and then everything went quiet. After one hour, perhaps an hour and a half, somebody started to shout, to cry, "Adila, Adila, get me some water." And then again, we could hear curses and somebody asked if anyone was still alive. And then we heard shots and everything went quiet again. Everybody was silent. I forgot to tell you that they had asked about wounded. They wanted to know if anybody was wounded, and they said that there would be an ambulance that would take them to the hospital. So the wounded people crawled out, and they were killed immediately outside the warehouse. When this guy who was crying for water was killed, nobody spoke a word in the warehouse. Then we heard a sound and I thought that the vehicles were passing on the asphalt road and I could tell that the sound was approaching but I didn't know what was happening. When it became dark, we heard voices, "Cover the asphalt with the hay," and that there was a truck that arrived and somebody said, "It's enough for today." So they covered the whole area with hay and I thought they wanted to set it on fire, but they didn't. When it became dark, I realised that nobody was alive in the warehouse. I couldn't hear a single voice, a single sound. So I began to crawl out, and I sat down. But I was so weak and I couldn't -- couldn't leave. I just sat there for about one hour, an hour and a half. I was trying to stretch a little bit to get my bearings. But then at one point I had heard a whisper and I didn't know whether it was coming from inside the warehouse or outside the warehouse, because I was sitting next to a door. And I tried to walk across those dead bodies towards the whisper and I found two persons in the warehouse and I told them let's flee, let's get out of here. One of them was very young, he was a tall guy and he said we couldn't go together. I said, "I don't know where to go. I don't know where I am." But he said, "We couldn't go together." And I asked him where he was from. He said he was from Lolici. And I wanted to go with him, because he knew the area. But he kept telling me that we couldn't go together. So I wanted to know where the other guy was from and he addressed him by his first name, but he told me that this other person couldn't hear very well. So I stood up, I wanted to go with them, but they wouldn't let me. So I came out and I was standing behind the excavator. It was a very bright night, and the visibility was very good. All of a sudden, somebody said [indiscernible] and I heard a soldier and at one point, I lied down. And the voice said, "Get up." But I kept lying down. And he went on like that for about two or three times and then he said, "Stand up." And all of a sudden I jumped up, and I went -- I left the warehouse which was on my left-hand side and I went towards the river, towards the brook where I drank some water.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness, at this point I want to ask you a few questions about what happened in the warehouse. I know that you're now talking about your escape from the warehouse. So if you could just listen to a few questions that I have about the warehouse. Now, you said in your evidence that when the shooting subsided, you went and hid. You reached an outside gate, a reception booth. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: In the warehouse. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was getting out of the warehouse? When I left it?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: No. I want you to think about when you were actually in the warehouse, and I think you survived by hiding in a reception booth.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You were in a sort of an office --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a kind of reception booth, yes, rather like that, a small hut.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And it was inside the warehouse.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was. Next to the warehouse, attached to the warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Was it inside the warehouse building or was it outside, completely outside the warehouse?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the warehouse I entered that reception booth. It was all under one roof, but it was separate from the warehouse where the dead were. But there were some dead there too, inside the warehouse where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, in the reception booth, you covered yourself with a dead body; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: A body, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And do you recall how long you lay under that dead body?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I lay there for 24 hours, in the warehouse, under a dead body. I was brought to the warehouse on a Thursday, about 4.00, 4.30, and the next Friday, on the 14th, I left the warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you see any of the concrete floor around you, or were there bodies covering the whole floor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: No where could you stand on the concrete floor without stepping on a dead body. The dead bodies had covered the entire concrete.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And your clothes, did you have blood on your clothes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I brought my sweater to Zivinice, which was bloodstained, when this Muskic from Cerska, when he was killed at Baljkovica. And there were people who saw how bloodstained my sweater was. I couldn't throw it away because it was cold at night, but it stank to me, never mind other people, but still I had to put it on again. And I reached Zepa with it, and from Zepa, with that sweater, I got to Zivinice.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that when you walked out of the factory, you saw an excavator; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. When we went out, I heard someone say that they were collecting the dead and loading them onto this truck. And when they were washing the asphalt, it was covered in blood, so they brought the water tank to wash it. And what we heard was the loading of the dead onto the truck. Where they took them, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Was there a time when you feared that you would be loaded alive onto a truck with all of these bodies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: What normal person would not be afraid? I kept thinking, why didn't I get killed, or I might get loaded onto the truck alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you hear the excavator loading bodies? Did you hear the engines of the excavator loading bodies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I heard it loading, only I didn't know what it was until they said that the excavator should park.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, I think you've already explained to the Judges that there came a time when you escaped from out of the warehouse and a Serb soldier saw you as you were crossing the road; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: We weren't crossing the road. I reached the road; he was to the right of the asphalt road, I was on the left-hand side when he stopped me. I lay down. The third time he yelled "Get up," I jumped up, I ran towards the river, the warehouse was left behind me to the left, and there wasn't a shot fired behind me. I didn't hear him shout "Stop" again. I crossed the river to some maize fields.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness, when you say that "he" yelled at you and "he" said get up, are you referring to the Bosnian Serb soldier?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I imagine it was a soldier. Why he didn't shoot, whether he thought it was one of them -- I believe he must have thought it was one of them, because they were 100 per cent sure that there was not a living soul left in the warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, the next part of your evidence you simply need to answer my questions yes or no. I think you eventually managed to get to the town of Zepa on the 26th of July, with some of your colleagues; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: But for five days I was in Podbrdze and then I reached Zepa. This person new Podbrdze well, the one who escaped with me. For five days he led me around Podbrdze. If it hadn't been for him, I would have never got out. He knew the ground; he knew every village. And every night we tried to cross the asphalt road but they were controlling it all night and all day. So during the night we would go into the woods and they would cry out, "Come on, balija, come down." They swore at Alija. Then they would call out Muslim names, "Zulfa," "Mustafa," "Alija, come on, come down. Surrender. No one will hurt you." I thought they must have noticed someone. So we couldn't cross the road. I tried to persuade him to go to Zepa. He wouldn't. He knew the road to Baljkovica. We reached a place called Jela. We found some more of our men there; I knew some of them. I tried to persuade them to go to Zepa, that we should go together. Then one of them answered, "My child is hungry, he will die of hunger." "He will die anyway if there is no food, I said." One man was wounded. A bullet had entered here [indicates] and come out here [indicates] but no real damage was done. He was a relative. He told me that there was a forester who had a transistor radio and that Zepa still hadn't fallen. So I said, "Let's go to Zepa." This one from Cerska wouldn't. He insisted on going to Cerska. While we were sitting there in a garden, we were looking for apples or pears or anything to eat, we heard bursts of fire above the village of Jela. These bursts of fire were heard, we hid, and then somebody appeared in an olive-grey shirt, with a long beard. I thought it was a Serb soldier. Then I pointed my finger at him, to this one from Cerska, but he said, "No, no, he's one of us." Then two came, both were deaf and dumb, and they stayed on with this man from Cerska. And then me and two others headed towards Zepa. They asked me, "Do you know the way?" I said, "I don't. If only I could see Rogac, then I would be able to find my way." And so we went through the woods. Up above Jela, on a hilltop, we saw eight dead. Those dead were found when they went to collect the bones. I told them where we had seen them. I reached Rogac. I should have crossed Koprivne, which I knew very well because I went hunting there. I had to go around a house that had some very dangerous watchdogs. I heard a voice. The three of us went to the right. We sat down in a grass field, and after four or five minutes, I saw two men appearing where we had been. I didn't say anything to the others. Then one of them noticed and said, "Look. Do you see that?" And I said, "I do." "What are we going to do?" "Well, they can't see us." And when the two of them headed towards us, across the field -- the grass hadn't been cut and they were heading towards us. So I said, "Let's run," and then the other said, "Well, let's see, maybe they are ours." And then I said, "Well, how come we are here?" They came up close, then the last one slipped and I saw that he had something on his back and I realised he was one of ours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness, I realise that the trip that you made to Zepa was very difficult and very frightening, but I would just like you to simply confirm a number of points to the Judges by simply answering yes or no. Otherwise, I think we're going to be here a very long time, and I know you want to go home to Bosnia tomorrow. So simply answer yes or no. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why should I say yes or no to your questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you arrive in Zepa on the 26th of July.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 26th of July, I arrived in Zepa, about 3.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And then I think, on the 29th of July, Zepa fell, you --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 29th, Zepa fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You left Zepa and you spent a long time -- Witness, listen to my question and simply answer yes or no to the question. I think you left Zepa on the 29th of July and you spent over 40 days wandering in Bosnian Serb territory, and then you eventually made your way to the free territory on the 17th of September of 1995. Is that right? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness J, you are now going to answer questions that Mr. Petrusic, the Defence counsel, is going to put to you. Mr. Petrusic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, and good morning, Your Honours, my learned friends opposite.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. I shall do my best, in the course of this examination, not to take you back too much to your experiences, terrible experiences, and as a wise man, I hope we will understand one another and be able to cooperate well. Before I begin with my questions, I should like to raise a purely technical matter so as to facilitate the work of the interpreters and all of us here present, and that is that when I put a question to you, as we speak the same language, could you wait a couple of seconds before giving your answer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Witness J, at the beginning of your testimony, you said that the assembly of Muslim men was held in Jaglici.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And only able-bodied men attended.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were men; there were boys of 15 to 17 years of age.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did anyone of the military leaders of Srebrenica give you an order to gather at Jaglici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were informed by couriers that Srebrenica was to fall. On that day, I spent the day collecting hay. The couriers came, "Srebrenica has fallen. The old men, women, and children are going to Potocari and the others to the woods." The assembly was held at Jaglici, so we rallied there on the 11th, in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: If we can call this an order to go into the woods, was it accepted by all the men who had rallied there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it was accepted to go towards Tuzla and be what may.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: There were no opposite opinions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not able to notice any. We were there. I went from Jaglici, on the 12th, at twenty to one.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps know, or did you perhaps hear from men who went through all this with you that there was a conflict in Jaglici between two different currents of members of the 28th Division?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between whom and whom, do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: That there were two groups. One group was in favour of Potocari and the other was in favour of making a breakthrough.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was above Ravne Njive. Those who had to go to Potocari went to Potocari, and those who went into the woods went towards Jaglici. At Ravne Njive they separated from their families, who went to Potocari, and we went towards Jaglici.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that you separated from your families. But when you rallied at Jaglici, were there any incidents there, and even weapons being used by various commanders?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: At Jaglici there were no incidents while I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness J. Buljim Brdo was within the enclave, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And access to it was not open to Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: We crossed their lines. I didn't see anyone there, on their lines. I saw their bunkers and trenches very well, but I didn't see any soldiers, until we reached a macadam road below Buljim. When we got there, the column was stopped. Some asked, "What are we waiting for?" And they said that the column had been broken up and then the shooting started.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So at Buljim, where their front line was, there was no one.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether they had moved away and hid, I don't know. But anyway, I didn't see anyone at Buljim. I just saw the bunkers and the trenches but no soldiers, no one alive. No persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Witness J, at the beginning of your testimony on Friday, if my memory serves me, you said that when searching you, the Serb soldiers took 100 German marks.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave 100 German marks involuntarily. When I wandered to the asphalt, there were two of them standing there, they searched our pockets, our belts. They told us to put our hands behind our heads and said, "Give us your money." I had 100 marks here in my pocket and I gave them the 100 marks. But I had some more in the lining of my jacket, and they found this, 600 marks, two necklaces, and ten gold coins.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You said that the column, when it was formed four by four, that according to your estimate, it was 400 to 500 metres long.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Who accompanied it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was accompanied or escorted by Serb soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did you notice anything in particular about the way it was escorted?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't notice anything, except when we got close to Kravica, I saw an UNPROFOR personnel carrier. Who was on it, I don't know. Whether it was the Serbs or UNPROFOR. But in any event they didn't do anything. We passed by it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: At the front of that column, was there a soldier with a dog?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he had a dog and he had a 53 or an 84 rifle. I'm not sure because he was quite a way from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You mean a light machine-gun, don't you, an M-53 or M-54 or M-84?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Witness J, when you entered this warehouse, a picture of which is on the ELMO, could you tell us the size of that warehouse? I know it is difficult to think back and remember these things.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my estimate, it seemed to me between 40 and 50 metres long and maybe 15 metres wide.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So 40 to 50 metres long?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You said that the Serb soldiers entered. As far as I understood your testimony, they opened the door and fired.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: They fired through the door and they threw grenades through the windows and used rifle grenades, and all sorts of things. It was really a disaster. I don't know what kind of a nation they can be to kill people like that. Let everyone live as they will.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did you say they were using Zoljas?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: They used anything at all, whatever they could get hold of.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Witness J, I assure you that it is not my intention to revive those terrible memories for you, but I have to, so could you explain. You were a soldier?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: A Zolja is a deadly weapon or ammunition that destroys man, personnel and causes burning in a closed area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one needs to ask me anything. There's proof on the walls and the blood samples, and they have proven everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm just asking you whether what I'm saying is correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I heard firing was not just automatic weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Witness J, could you explain why, in fact, you went into the woods?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went into the woods. I had to go somewhere to save my life, as anyone else would do to get a hold of free territory. I already had occasion to see since 1992 what was done in the places that fell before Srebrenica. There was burning and killing regardless of whether people were young or old. They hit cows and calves. My daughter was watching the cattle. One of them was wounded. Why is he shooting my daughter if I am on the front line? She is innocent.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Witness J, do you know that from the other -- the Muslim side, the same things were done?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. What did we have, and what did they have? They were sitting on the -- on Rogac, like a gentleman, whether he wants to shoot Zepa or I don't know what he could do. What about us? We started defending ourselves with hunting rifles, with homemade devices. Everything went to the Serb army. We were left without anything. You also know in that period -- we didn't have a tank or a personnel carrier or a mortar or a howitzer. They had everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in the period of spring, summer, autumn, winter of 1992 to 1993, that tens of villages and dozens of villagers were killed of Serb ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: We weren't the ones to start the war. We were attacked. We had to defend ourselves. That has been proven. They first attacked Slovenia and then Croatia and then Bosnia-Herzegovina and now they are attacking Kosovo, and now they want Sandzak too. It is an aggressor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Witness J, my question was focussed on the municipality of Srebrenica and the spring, summer, autumn of 1992 and the beginning of winter 1993 inclusive -- until the arrival of the UN mission or rather the formation of a protected zone. When it was protected, why did it let such a disaster happen? That is my question. Do you know that in that area and in that period, dozens of Serb villages were burnt down and that hundreds of civilians were killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Understand what I'm saying. We had to defend ourselves. How many people surrendered in Vlasenica? Where are they today? It would have been the same with Srebrenica and Zepa. All they wanted was to destroy us so we wouldn't exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And these acts that were committed in that time and the area that we are referring to, did they have the same aim in mind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: If the Serbs wanted to destroy the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did we Muslims attack the Serbs or did the Serbs attack Muslims? Who attacked whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: I don't want to take any more time. I'm just asking this witness to answer my question. Did it happen or did it not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: As they attacked us, we had to defend ourselves. That is number one. Only if we had the equipment they had, we wouldn't have acted in that way. We defended ourselves with hunting rifles and devices.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did you have infantry weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only had a hunting rifle throughout the war, and I brought it to Jaglici.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did you have an armed army, military unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who would arm them if somebody bought a weapon or captured a weapon. That's what they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So you are claiming that there were no infantry weapons or automatic rifles or machine-guns mortars?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: In our local community, there wasn't a single light machine-gun. We may have had eight carbines and hunting rifles. And perhaps somebody prior to the war may have purchased an automatic rifle. That's all we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Your Honours, I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, very much, Mr. Petrusic. Mr. Cayley, any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Riad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness J. I'll have to call you J and not to call you by your name. We do appreciate your coming here to testify, and we fully realise how painful it is for you. I'll not prolong your ordeal, but we would like to see more clearly some of the events you mentioned in a few questions. I'll start by what you mentioned about your being in the Bosnian army. How long did you stay in the Bosnian army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the 17th of April, 1992 until 1996.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And what was your grade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have any. I simply went to the line, I was there. I was a member of the civil -- before I was a member of the civil protection service, I worked in the logistics department and it was like that until 1996 when I was demobilised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But you said that on the 11th of July, 1995, you were a farmer in the village in this Srebrenica enclave. Was that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I had been working on my land all my life. This was my source of income.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, we go to the warehouse. I'm sorry if I have to evoke your memory, and the memory because there is some kind of -- it doesn't look very clear to me what happened there. You said the warehouse was so full that a match would not fall on the ground, it would fall on the head of people. And then during these events --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Apparently nobody was left alive after they were killed, I mean how were they killed. I mean killing people who were sticking to each other. How was it? Was it through a bomb? How could you kill a place and nobody was left? Can I just ask you this very sad memory, how it happened? Was it by grenades, was it by -- because you can't shoot people standing almost totally stuck to each other.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Take the example of the men who left the warehouse with me. He had been hit with shrapnel all over his body, on his legs. I wasn't wounded at all. So he managed to reach Baljkovica and he was killed, that's where he died. But I had not been wounded. I was just lucky. It was my fate, that I survived. When we were going to Zepa there were four of us in a column. Actually, there were nine of us. I was the fourth one in the column, and the one behind stepped on a mine. And the one who was the seventh in the column also stepped on a mine and lost two legs. Afterwards, when they went back to the area to look for the bodies, look for the bones, they managed to find those bodies as they were clearing up the road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You mentioned that -- when you were answering the Defence counsel, you mentioned that the Serbs shot people young and old as well as animals, as well as the cat, I suppose, you mentioned --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: -- why did they have to collect people in the warehouse. They can shoot them everywhere. Did they shoot people wherever they found them, and whether they are; men, women?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was walking around in Pobude, I saw a number of dead bodies in brooks and rivers. They just wanted to get rid of people. They didn't pay attention to whether somebody was young or old. They just wanted to destroy them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: What happened to your daughter?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: My daughter was watching after cattle in a field. There was another girl with her from a neighbouring village, and shelling took place and one of my daughters was killed and the other one was wounded. The girl who was from the neighbouring village was also wounded. She didn't manage to reach Srebrenica alive, but the other one spent 17 days in the hospital and she survived. One of my oxen was killed, a cow was also killed in that shelling. Everything was destroyed. I have lost a number of relatives and cousins and people who could have helped me, but today I have to help their children, and it's very difficult for me to help anyone. I am barely surviving.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: We are very happy that you have survived.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was lucky. Yes, that's what I keep telling myself. But what's it worth now? My life has been damaged, my health. When I have to sit for a long time and then when I have to stand up, it's very difficult for me to stand up on my right leg from rheumatism.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Well, I think that will pass with time. You're still a young man.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I were allowed to go back to my land, yes, but they wouldn't let me go back. And lots of criminals are still at large and the world is simply watching, and the world could have helped us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: The world is listening very carefully to what you are saying, so be fully aware of that. Now, just my last question: Those people who were in this warehouse, all of them, were they soldiers, were they military people, or were they civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were civilians, most of them. Most of them were very young children, elderly people. There were people of 60 years of age or more. They didn't dare go to Potocari. They thought it would be easier for them to go through the woods.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You mean they collected them from the woods?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who collected them? They were capturing them in the woods, and then they took them to Lolici, and after they had been gathered in Lolici, from there they were taken to Kravica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: That's the answer I wanted. Thank you so much, and I wish you luck.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judge Riad. Judge Wald.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Witness J, you told us that when Srebrenica fell, a courier came to tell people, and it had been agreed upon that the men would go through the woods, and the women and children and others would go on to Potocari. Now, had that kind of agreement been arrived at by the leaders of the Muslim community in Srebrenica, or was it, as the Defence counsel suggested, an order from the members of the 28th Brigade or the Muslim army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: They informed the civilians, the population in the villages, that Srebrenica had fallen, and they said that we should go to the woods or to Potocari. There were two options and we could choose between the two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Who is the "they" that told you that? What do you mean by "they"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably the United Nations who were protecting Srebrenica, they probably said that Srebrenica had fallen, that the enclave had fallen, and then our people conveyed the message to us, our superiors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: "Superiors" meaning your superiors in the Bosnian army or your leaders in the community?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably those who represented the municipality, the municipal authorities. They told the military and the civilians that Srebrenica had fallen and that we should leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. At the time that you left, were you still a member of the Bosnian army? Even though you were farming your land, you were still in the Bosnian army when you left to go to the woods?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was a member of the civilian defence when I left, and then after about -- I spent about three months in the civilian defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. When you were going through the woods and you met your first and second ambushes that you told us about, was the first firing by the Serb armies, or did, in any case, the men in the woods initiate the fire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: It mostly came from the left side of the hill. We could hear someone shouting, "What are you waiting for?" and then they cursed at us and at that moment shooting started. Lots of people remained there, lots of wounded and dead. But nobody paid attention to anybody else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Did some of the people in the column that was marching towards Tuzla, did they return the fire? When they were shot at, did they shoot back?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody returned fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Nobody returned fired.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody even thought of returning fire --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- because we were surrounded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Now, my next question deals with when General Mladic came. I want to make sure I have the dates right. General Mladic, I think you said, but you can tell me if I'm wrong, he came on the 13th and assured the people gathered there in the field that you would be taken care of and given shade and given food, et cetera. Was that the 13th? And then on the 14th was when the shooting --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 13th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Right. And then on the 14th, the shooting occurred in the warehouse; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 14th was the shooting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So that was the day after General Mladic --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Mladic arrived on Thursday, in Lolici, and on Thursday we were brought to the warehouse. The shooting started on Thursday, around 4.00 or 5.00 in the afternoon. And on Friday, that is, on the 14th, I spent the whole day in the warehouse. On the night between Friday and Saturday, I left the warehouse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in the warehouse, I think you told Judge Riad, in answer to one of his questions, that there were a lot of men collected from the column, from the woods, who had either surrendered or been captured. To the best of your knowledge -- to the best of your -- could I --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Columns of people were brought in from the woods. We didn't get there altogether. People kept arriving in groups, because we had surrendered up in the hills and people started brandishing white shirts on sticks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: But to your knowledge, to the best of your knowledge, were all the people in the warehouse people who had either been captured or surrendered in the woods? None of them were people who had stayed in Potocari and were bused out of Potocari. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Nobody from Potocari was there. Just people who had gone to the woods, they were there in the warehouse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: What happened in other places, I don't know. I just know what happened when we were surrounded at Kamenica. I don't know what happened to other people. Whether they had surrendered or whether they had been captured, I don't know. I just know what happened where I was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Now, my last question is: You said that you got back to Zepa on September 26th. Now, when you got back there, was Zepa still under siege? That was before its surrender on the 29th. Was it under assault and being besieged by the Serbian forces when you got there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge of how long it had been under siege before that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't on the 29th. Zepa fell on the 29th of July, not September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. I see. So Zepa had fallen already in July.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in July, on the 29th of July. And it was on the 26th that I reached Zepa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Of September.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: In September I left for Tuzla. It was on the 9th of September that I left for Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Just to clarify it once and for all, when did you get to Zepa? When did you reach Zepa?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I reached Zepa on the 26th of July, around 3.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. So my question, then, still is: Was Zepa under siege, or had it already surrendered by the time you got there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, it had not surrendered yet on the 26th of the July. The last convoy left Zepa on the 26th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. So do you know how long Zepa had been under military siege by the time you got there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the 29th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: No, but when had it begun? Do you know when the siege, the military siege, of Zepa had begun?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: It began, I mean the attack on Zepa, as soon as Srebrenica fell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So that would have been around July 10th or 11th. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness J, let me turn the situation a little bit. You said that the fate had it so that you survived. Let me try to tell you something. You are here with us, you have told us a story, and you have a story to tell to the world so that these terrible things could be avoided, independent of who is responsible for them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, Your Honour, very much. I'm in favour of that as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'm very glad to hear that we share the same opinion, Witness J. Thank you very much for coming here to testify. We hope that you will continue to be witness of these terrible events, and I hope that by doing so you will do a great service to humanity. Thank you very much once again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cayley, I don't think we have any exhibits to take care of. Mr. Petrusic, I don't think that there's anything that we should settle in that respect. Could the usher please show the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Harmon, what is next, or Mr. Cayley?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Sorry. You said "Mr. Harmon," so I thought my colleague would answer. We do have another witness, Mr. President, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Any protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: He will be known by a pseudonym, and he will have the same protection as this last witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the conditions are the same as for this witness. Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We agree to that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. For the public, let me just say that it will be a public session. Mr. Cayley, you may sit down. Witness J, please do not move. We will leave the courtroom and you will leave the courtroom after that. For now, we will have a 20-minute break, after which we will resume the hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, would you please read the solemn declaration that the usher will give you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, you may be seated now. Mr. Dubuisson. Mr. Dubuisson is going to show you a piece of paper with your name written on it. Could you please have a look at the piece of paper and tell us by saying simply yes or no if this is, indeed, your name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this is your name, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well then, Witness, you will first answer questions that will be put to you by Mr. Cayley who is on your right-hand side. Let me just thank you for coming to the International Tribunal. Mr. Cayley, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness, for your protection, I will be addressing you as Witness K throughout your evidence. Witness, you are Bosnian by nationality; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you were born a Muslim by faith; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: In July of 1995, you were inside the Srebrenica enclave; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes, in 1995, I was in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And at the time you were a member of the Bosnian army inside the Srebrenica enclave; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes. I was a member of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Inside the Srebrenica enclave, can you describe to the Judges what kind of army the Bosnian army was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: There was an army, but we didn't have much weaponry. We started to defend ourselves in the war with hunting rifles. And in doing so, we would seize weapons from Bosnian Serbs from time to time, and we would use those weapons to defend ourselves. The soldiers that were in Srebrenica, I mean the army that was in Srebrenica, was not a disciplined army. The United Nations were there, and we were not allowed to hold our lines because they had their checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness, did you have a uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: No. No. I never put on a uniform. I was never issued with a uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What weapon were you armed with in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: I didn't have any weapon. They were in warehouses, what weapons there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What was the name of the unit to which you belonged, the name of the Bosnian army unit to which you belonged?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: 282nd Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I want you now to think back to the 11th of July of 1995. And I think on that day, you set off towards Jaglici; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think you then started to make your way in a very large column towards Tuzla and the free territory; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: (redacted),

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 8/A/2.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I know that the journey through the woods was a very difficult one and that there was shooting and there was explosions, and a large number of people were killed, but I would like you to move forward in time to the point where you, and a large group of other men, surrendered to the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: But, first of all, if the exhibit could be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And if you could indicate to the Judges what is represented by the dotted line on that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: This is the village of Jaglici [indicates] and this is where we crossed the line. There used to be a UN checkpoint here, and to our right where we crossed the line that was held by Bosnian Serbs. This is where we crossed the line [indicates]. There were many people in the column one by one. We had set off through the woods in the direction of Tuzla. I will show you the route we took. This is the way where we went [indicates], and this is just approximately. And we surrendered to the Bosnian Serbs at Konjevic Polje at this place here. This is where we crossed the asphalt road, and we were assembled here on a meadow.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And let the record show that the witness has indicated on Prosecutor's Exhibit 8A/2 that the dotted line on that map represents the approximate route that he took through the forest on the 12th and 13th of July, and that where that dotted line bisects the road between Konjevic Polje and Bratunac, which runs through Kravica, is the point at which he surrendered to the Serbs on the 13th of July. Now, Witness, if you could tell the Judges what happened to you after you surrendered to the Serbs on the 13th of July. And if you would speak for a minute, minute and a half and then take a pause, I may have a few questions to ask you to clarify your testimony, or I may just ask you to proceed on with your story. Can you do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes, I can. After we crossed the asphalt road, they searched us, and we were moving in a column one by one. They were taking away our money, our gold, watches; everything we had that was of any value. We had backpacks with food, but none of us had any weapons. Those who had weapons had thrown them away in the woods. We didn't dare surrender with weapons. So we gathered in a meadow, and there were quite a few of us. I was in the first column, and I think that we were about 1.000 in that column, approximately. I cannot tell you the exact number of people in the column at that moment, so this is just an estimate. They were standing around us, and we sat down, one next to the other, and we were facing the asphalt road. On my right-hand side, in a corner where people were sitting, there was a tank, and on the right side of the tank there was a Praga, which would, from time to time, open fire and shell in the direction of the woods. They were firing mortars but I couldn't see them. They must have been near the houses that were to my left side. There were many wounded amongst us. There were also children of maybe 14 or 15 years of age. They selected younger people, and they also stopped buses that were coming from the area of Potocari, towards Kladanj, evacuating people. Those young boys would be then put onto buses and sent towards Kladanj. There were lots of wounded amongst us, and they were being taken away to some houses that were situated some 50 metres away from us, on our right-hand side, maybe more, to protect them from the heat. It was very hot on that day. Then at one point they would sprinkle us with water from a water tank; I remember they did that on three occasions. From time to time somebody would go to fetch water. Mostly it was younger boys who would go to get water because they didn't allow older people to leave the group. We spent a couple of hours sitting in the meadow, and then the second column arrived, the Bosnian Serbs brought the second column of people. Some had helmets, some had some kind of caps, multicoloured uniforms, and they were armed with automatic weapons, automatic rifles. On our left side, next to the houses, there was an anti-aircraft gun, a three-barrelled anti-aircraft gun, which was also firing in the direction of the woods, where we had come from. After that, after the second column had arrived, I recognised two men who were from Skelani, from my neighbourhood. They were two brothers, Ahmed and Dzemo, and they were put away -- they were separated and put next to the tank. I knew them because they were my -- they knew them because they were their neighbours. And the others were placed in the same meadow where we were. One man tried to escape, one of us. He had accompanied a wounded man towards the house, which was on our right side, but they managed to catch him. They captured him and they brought him to the tank, and the one who was driving the tank came to him and he hit him with his fist. The man fell down and fainted. The other group, the people who had arrived in the meantime, I don't know who they were, maybe some members of the special forces from the Serbian army, but as far as I could tell, they were respected by others. I could tell by the attitude of other soldiers that they were respected. They had kind of black T-shirts with short sleeves; they had brand new boots, uniforms. Their commander, who was ahead of us, who was standing in front of us, kept brandishing his knife and he said that he would take revenge upon us for his brother who had lost his life in the war. He didn't touch anyone; he just played with his knife. But when people would bring water, we were very thirsty, he would fire a bullet or two from his automatic rifle to calm us down because at that moment we would run towards the water because we were thirsty. The one who was wearing a black T-shirt, at one point, took an automatic rifle, with a round clip which can hold much more ammunition, I don't know how much exactly, he approached the soldier who had been hit near the tank and he stood above him and he simply fired several bursts of gunfire in his chest. And then he ordered two men from my group who were there in the meadow, two Muslims, to come out and to throw him away some 20 or 30 metres away from us in the meadow.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness, that's a good point for you to pause. I just have a number of questions to ask you, to clarify what you've already said. Now, you said in your evidence that when you arrived at the meadow that "they searched us" and "they were standing around". You mean by that Bosnian Serb soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes, I mean the Bosnian Serb soldiers. They searched us. They took everything of value, money, gold, watches, valuables, and backpacks, and they threw them all into a pile. They would search each of the soldiers to make sure there were no weapons. And we had to sit in the meadow; we were surrounded to make sure that we wouldn't disperse.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, these Bosnian Serb soldiers, how were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: They had camouflage uniforms on. Some of them had helmets, some had caps, some had nothing on their heads, like me, for instance. They had bulletproof jackets; some were camouflage and some were SMB or olive-grey.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Then you described another unit that were wearing black uniforms and you said that that unit was respected by the other soldiers. How long after you arrived in the meadow did the soldiers that were dressed in black arrive?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: A couple of hours later, something like that. That's my impression, very approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, the soldier who shot the man next to the tank, how was he dressed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: As I said, he took an automatic rifle from the man who was playing around with the knife and he killed this man of ours, a Muslim. He had a black, short-sleeved T-shirt on him and the trousers were camouflage; he had new boots. So that as far as I could have noticed, their own soldiers held them in high esteem. They were valued more than ordinary soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How, to the best of your memory, were all of the Muslim men who were sitting in that meadow dressed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: They were all in civilian clothes. I didn't notice anyone wearing a camouflage uniform or a part of a military uniform. They were all in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Were there people amongst you that were wounded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: There were. There were wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: After a couple of hours, what was the state of these wounded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Some of those wounded, because it was extremely hot, as I just said, they sprayed us with water from a tank on three occasions, they cooled us off so we wouldn't faint, and these wounded men, I saw quite a number of them faint. And whoever was next to them would pour water over them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, after the arrival of the second group of Muslim men, can you estimate how many men there were in the meadow?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: You mean in all?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Approximately how many men there were in the meadow.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Perhaps around 3.500 to 4.000, that's my estimate, maybe 3.000, 3.500, 4.000. I don't know exactly. I didn't count them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: After the men in the black uniform, the Bosnian Serb soldiers in the black uniforms had arrived, what is the next significant event that you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: We were all facing the road in the meadow and watching to see what would happen to us. We were all in great fear and panic. The tank driver climbed the anti-aircraft gun and pointed towards us as if he would shoot, but he didn't. He would merely intimidate us. And then buses from Srebrenica arrived with the women, children, and the elderly, heading towards Kladanj, and I recognised a number of women in the buses as they went by. And the younger persons, there were some girls in the meadows too. The buses would be halted and they would be boarded onto the buses, and they left towards Kladanj. After that, after a while, I don't know how long, General Mladic arrived with his bodyguards, maybe five or six men, and he stayed there for maybe 10 or 15 minutes in the meadow, roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did General Mladic say anything to you while he was in the meadow?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: He addressed us. I cannot remember the exact words he used. He addressed us, saying that nothing wrong would happen, not to be afraid, that they were good, that not a hair on a head would be hurt, that we would all be exchanged for their Serbs, that we would be evacuated to Tuzla or Kladanj, that we would all rejoin our families in safety, and that we should not worry at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: After General Mladic left, do you recall what happened to you next?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: After that, I don't know after how long exactly, this commander who was standing in front of us all that time with a knife in his hand, he would select us, the more able-bodied amongst us, and he would say, "You, you, and you," pointing a finger at us, and we would go out and he would say that we would be exchanged for their Serbs, "who was imprisoned by your Muslims," as he said. "we're exchanging you for our Serbs," that's what he said to us. And then we got to the road. Buses were waiting for us, two to three buses. I was among those who were in the bus. We were loaded, very many of us. It was so hot, it was stifling, and I noticed immediately that the bus wasn't taking us towards Konjevic Polje or Kladanj, but rather that we were going in the direction of Bratunac. And then after I don't know how many minutes, it wasn't a long ride, the bus took a turning to the right and they drove us in front of a warehouse of some sort. That was Kravica.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 8/3. If that could be placed on the ELMO, please, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness, do you recognise this place? Can you just identify the location?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: I know this place very well. I'll show you now where they took us and where we got off.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you could just wait one moment, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you tell the Judges the name of this place, if you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: This place is called Kravica. Before the war, in peacetime, I would pass by here often, but I never noticed those warehouses then. I know that I was close to Kravica. Maybe this was not the centre of Kravica that I was familiar with. I think this place is called Sandici or Kravica, between Konjevic Polje and Sandici. And so we were driven there to Kravica, to these warehouses.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could now be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 8A/2.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you said, Witness, in your evidence, that you thought that you were being taken to the free territory, you were taken to be exchanged. But then you realised that the buses turned in the wrong direction and went to Bratunac. Could you indicate to the Judges in which direction you drove when the buses left on the map that you see in front of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: From here towards Bratunac [indicates]. That was the direction we took.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So let the record show that on Prosecutor's Exhibit 8A/2 that the witness travelled from the dotted line that crosses the road between Konjevic Polje and Bratunac to Kravica.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And after you'd been told that you were to be exchanged, where did you think that you should have been going? Where should the Serbs have taken you if they were to exchange you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Towards Kladanj [indicates]. In this direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let the record show on Prosecutor's Exhibit 8A/2 that the witness is indicating from where the dotted line bisects the road at Konjevic Polje towards Konjevic Polje. And, in fact, the direction is indicated by an arrow pointing towards Konjevic Polje. If the witness could now be shown a new exhibit which is 1/19. Mr. Registrar, on this exhibit, the witness has placed his name and signed it because it was attached to a statement.
