So if the redacted copy to be placed on the ELMO and the copy with the signature and the name of the witness can be placed in front of the witness, that way the witness will remain protected.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Witness, this, I believe, is a diagram that you drew for the investigators from the Office of the Prosecutor in 1998 showing the approximate locations of buildings at the Kravica warehouse complex; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you indicate, first of all, to the Judges, the building that you were taken into by just pointing to that building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: I can [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let the record show on Prosecutor's Exhibit 1/19 that the witness pointed to the large rectangle nearest the road between Konjevic Polje and Bratunac which is parallel to that road and has two smaller boxes beneath it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The two smaller boxes, Witness, one with the cross in it, could you inform the Judges what they are below the building to which you were taken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: What do you mean below the building? Above the building?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: There's a box which indicates the factory into which you were taken. Below that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: There are two small boxes, and one has a cross inside it. Can you explain to the Judges what they represent?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: These are buses [indicates] that drove us there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let the record show that the three small rectangular boxes on this diagram, on Prosecutor's Exhibit 1/19, that the witness has indicated are buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, the box with the cross inside it, what does the cross represent?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: This is the bus [indicates] that I was in. And when they quickly ordered us to get off as quickly as we could and enter the warehouse, there's an opening here, and that is the one I went through. So they unloaded us there, and we were told to get inside as quickly as we possibly could.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And finally if the witness could be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 8/1. And if that could be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, do you remember, Witness, yesterday I showed you this photograph, and I indicated to you that it was aerial imagery that had been taken on the 13th of July of 1995 at the Kravica warehouse at the time that you were there. The two white boxes below the warehouse, can you tell the Judges what you told me they were yesterday when you saw this photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: There are two buses here [indicates], and we came from this direction [indicates]. Then we turned right and we passed this warehouse [indicates], then another right turn and then a left turn. When I got off, I saw some warehouses were there. We were unloaded from the buses and we went inside, and I confirm, personally, that that is the exact spot where I was. I was in that warehouse here just in front of this first bus I got off and went in.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let the record show that the witness, although I think it's quite clear from the transcript, identified that the two rectangular white boxes immediately in front of the warehouse are the buses which he drew on the diagram which he provided to the Office of the Prosecutor. And that he confirmed that the bus on the right-hand side of the photograph is the bus from which he alighted and that is where he entered into the warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could now have, I think, Prosecutor's Exhibit 8/4, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Witness, what is this a photograph of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: It's the warehouse that I was in.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you indicate the door through which you entered the warehouse?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: I can [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let the record show that the witness is indicating the entrance on the extreme left of Prosecutor's Exhibit 8/4, it's on the extreme left of one of three entrances that are joined together.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness, were there any?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Mr. Cayley, for interrupting you. I have a small point of clarification. Can we go back to Exhibit 8/1? I think that the usher has that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, that's the aerial photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could it be possible to ask the witness where was the door of the bus through which he got on and got off the bus. On what side was it?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness, if you understood that question, could you do as the President asked and indicate the door on the bus from which you alighted into the factory?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: It was on the right-hand side. I can show you on the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Although I think the point is a little large, the witness is indicating that the door and, indeed, said the door on the bus was on the right-hand side of the bus. That's on Prosecutor's Exhibit 8/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If Prosecutor's Exhibit 8/4 could be placed on the ELMO again.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you've just explained to the Judges that you went into the warehouse on the left-hand side. And now I have a question for you: Were there Bosnian Serb soldiers in and around the warehouse?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you explain to the Judges how those soldiers were dressed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: I didn't know. When I entered the hangar, I didn't know that there were Bosnian Serb soldiers on guard duty around there. But when I escaped from the hangar, I jumped out of the window of the hangar, then I saw that there were guards. And I jumped out during the night, and I didn't see how they were dressed. I just saw those who were in front entering the warehouse during the daytime. They had camouflage uniforms, but one of them had a blue UN helmet on his head and they had flak jackets on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So these were Bosnian Serb soldiers that you could see as you were looking outwards from the inside of the factory?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes. And who would enter inside while we could see, it was still daylight.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, after you entered the factory, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: They shoved us into this warehouse. Where I was, it was full of men so that I was somewhere in the middle. I don't know exactly, as far as I could notice. They ordered us to sit down. We sat down as we could, one next to another. After that, I could see two younger men. They provoked us. They demanded that they make a confession they didn't know. After that, they brought them back to where they were. Then they took watches off people; gold, money, whatever people had, and they threatened us. If somebody failed to give up his money and money was found on him, he would be killed. And people who had anything, one by one, they went up and handed it over. I, too, personally, had little change, although they had taken my ring in the meadow, not my wedding ring, though, I had that too. I said it was a souvenir from my girlfriend, because it wasn't a wedding ring, it was a gold band. And I gave them my watch and the chain and this gold band, everything I had; I didn't have any money on me. And this applied to everyone. Whoever had anything, they handed it over. And they wrote it down on small bits of paper. When I went up and handed over these valuables, they would take down my name and surname, as if they would be so nice as to return those things to us one day, and then we would go back to the place where we had been before.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you said in your evidence that "they provoked us" and "they demanded that they make a confession they didn't know". Now, are you saying that Bosnian Serb soldiers demanded that Muslim men amongst you make confessions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes. They interrogated people, not many of them. I saw two young men being taken out. They were told to stand up against a wall. They shouted at them. They asked them about some places, I don't know which ones; I don't remember what we were interested in. But these two young men, of course, didn't know anything about that. They were not beaten; they were brought back to their places. From time to time they would bring water in buckets, in white buckets, with Jupol letters written on it, and we would then fight amongst ourselves for this water. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: (redacted) because we were sitting behind and we could never get any water. People would shout. We were all very thirsty. We had not been drinking or eating for quite some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness, how full of men, how packed was the section of the warehouse that you were in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: In my estimate, there were approximately 1.000, between 1.000 and 1.500 people, roughly. I'm not sure either. Maybe less, maybe more. This is just my rough estimate. This is how it seemed to me while I was there, inside, but I was in fear.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I understand that. How close was each man to the other inside the warehouse?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: One next to the other, shoulder by shoulder.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So each man was touching the other inside the factory building. There was no --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: There was no space between all of the men inside the factory at all.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: No, not at all. There was no space whatsoever. People were touching each other, they were sitting next to each other, so that nobody could walk between two people. Only if you lean on one side, one could perhaps walk slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What was the atmosphere like in the factory at this time? How did you all feel?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Terrible is all that I can say. We were in great panic, all of us. I was fearful. When we were brought there, I knew what was in store for us, I knew it already. I mean, as soon as we were crowded into those buses and when I realised that we were not going towards Tuzla but Bratunac, I knew what was happening, what would happen, especially when we were brought to the warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you've explained to the Judges that the Bosnian Serb soldiers took your belongings, that some interrogations took place. Can you recall what happened after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that very well. After that the night fell, it was in the evening. When we came there, it was still daylight. I don't know what time it was but it was getting dark. After it became dark, some shelling started. I heard shots and I realised that shells were falling around, and I heard a sizzling noise of shell fragment. And then they told us, "See how we're guarding you? We're not hitting you, we're not beating you. We're good to you. We'll let you go peacefully towards Tuzla, and your people are now shooting at us and they will not let you through peacefully." But I cannot believe, and I still don't believe, that our people were shooting at us. They didn't have any mortars. While we were going through the woods, I didn't see any mortar, any shells. We didn't have such things. So this created even greater panic, but after a while everything became quiet. They would take out two of our people, as if to -- they were saying that they needed them to pick up their wounded members because they didn't dare, they were afraid of being shot. I didn't see those people, I didn't see the people who were supposedly being brought by our people, by Muslims. They were simply being taken out two by two, and then they would be brought back. So after a while, after everything went quiet, they became very angry, the Bosnian Serbs. Four or five of them would enter the warehouse, yelling at us, shouting, cursing us, and this lasted for a while and then they became quiet. Some of them wanted to open fire on us, but there was one guy there who was wearing a multicoloured uniform and he had an automatic rifle in his hands, and he said, "Do not touch these people. It's not their fault. They're not guilty of anything." So this lasted for a while and then it became dark. At one point, while I was still in the warehouse, while it was still daylight -- I forgot to mention this -- buses were passing by, from Potocari, travelling in the direction of Kladanj, carrying women, children, and elderly, people who were being evacuated. So while buses were passing by, everything would be quiet. They didn't shout at us at that moment, but after a bus had gone by they would start yelling at us again. And then as I told you, after it became dark, one of them came in. He had a very long beard, dark sunglasses, he had very long curly hair, and he was the first one who opened fire from his automatic rifle on us, and I think that maybe three or four of us fell down immediately. The one wearing dark glasses was the first one to have opened fire. As soon as that happened, I threw myself on the ground and I fell down, and immediately after that chaos ensued.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I know that this was a terrible scene, but as best you can, if you can explain to the Judges what, if anything, you could see going on around you and for how long the shooting continued inside the warehouse.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: While I was inside the warehouse, they fired from all kinds of weapons. They first fired infantry weapons, automatic rifles. Then they would stop doing that. They would shoot for about half an hour, then take a little rest, and then there would be a new series of shooting. They would throw hand grenades through the windows, and grenades fell some two or three metres away from me. I could just feel the explosion, the detonation, and as a result of that I was injured by small shrapnel coming from those shells. So I got wounded, I was injured, but I felt well. I wasn't seriously injured. People started screaming, and it was terrible. It is hard for me to describe it. I haven't seen anything like it in any of the horror movies that I saw. This was far worse than any film. And this lasted all night long, with short breaks. Bosnian Serbs would take some rest, make a short break, and then they would resume. They opened fire from anti-aircraft weapons that were positioned on the asphalt road, with Zoljas as well. All I saw was some kind of lightning coming from weapons. A bullet hit me which came from, I believe, an infantry weapon, but I'm not sure. I was hit above my right knee. It was a gunshot wound but I didn't feel any pain. I was only concerned about losing my limb. I was worried that it might be a fragmentation bullet. After one of such breaks, when things became quiet, when they stopped shooting, I grabbed myself by my heel. I just wanted to make sure that my heel was there because for a while I couldn't feel it at all. And probably, it turned out later on, when I had some medical examination by medical specialists, that a tendon had been cut, and this is why I couldn't feel my heel for a while. But at the moment I grabbed it, I realised it was still there. I was glad it was there. I didn't feel any pain. It was just a slight burning feeling, as if from a cigarette. I don't know what time it was, but it was past midnight, things went quiet, and at that moment I tried to escape, I tried to leave the warehouse. There was a kind of container to my left, a kind of container that is part of a truck. It was not a big container. It was on the lower part of the wall. And above the container there was a window which was open, so I climbed onto the window and I jumped through the window.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness, can you describe the scene around you as you made your way to the window? Can you describe to the Judges what was on the floor all around you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: After the shooting, I felt a strange kind of heat, warmth, which was actually coming from the blood that covered the concrete floor, and I was stepping on the dead people who were lying around. But there were even people who were still alive, who were only wounded, and as soon as I would step on him, I would hear him cry, moan, because I was trying to move as fast as I could. I could tell that people had been completely disembodied, and I could feel bones of the people that had been hit by those bursts of gunfire or shells, I could feel their ribs crushing. And then I would get up again and I would continue towards the container. So I first made a few attempts, trying to figure out where exactly I could get out.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness, if you could pause there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, would it be an appropriate time to take a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Cayley. Thank you very much for your attention. We will have a 20-minute break now -- I'm sorry, half an hour break, a 30-minute break, so that the witness can have some rest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Cayley. You may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness, before the break, we had got to a point in time where you were trying to make your escape from the factory, and I just want to ask one question about a point in time before that. Do you recall when you were taken from the meadow to the factory at Kravica in a bus?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: In the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: On the bus, were there any guards? Were there any Bosnian Serb soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you describe how they were dressed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: In camouflage uniforms, camouflage.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you said, prior to the break, that there was a container in the warehouse which you were going to use to make good your escape. Can you explain to the Judges whereabouts this container was located inside the warehouse?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: What do you mean? In relation to me, where I was inside, or when you're looking inside from the entrance?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you could explain where the container was in relation to the back wall of the factory.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: I was roughly in the middle, and if I were to face the entrance that I passed through when I entered, the container was to my left, diagonally. Above the container were the windows, separated.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Judges how you used this container to make your escape?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: When everything was quiet again, I got up and I tried to save myself, to escape. So that I was treading on dead people, on the wounded. I reached the container. I looked to my right from where I had entered the warehouse. I saw outside that they were -- that there was some cigarettes lighted. All I could see was the cigarettes alight. They were Bosnian Serbs that were smoking cigarettes. I jumped because the container wasn't very high, so I was able to climb onto it. And then I stepped on to the window and jumped outside to the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 8/9, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Was there anything covering the window that you jumped through?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: No, it was open. It wasn't covered with anything. There were -- there was no glass in the window. It was open.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the exhibit could be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you can recall, could you indicate to the Judges which window it was that you jumped through?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: I don't know exactly which window now. I can roughly show you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: As best you can remember, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: It may have been one of these two [indicates], or maybe this one, the third one. One of these. One of these three or four. I don't know exactly which one it was because I wasn't looking when I jumped. I didn't remember. I didn't turn around to look at the windows.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So let the record show on Prosecutor's Exhibit 8/9 that the witness indicated that the window that he jumped through was one -- I think he was most certain about the three small windows on the back of this building, so -- this is actually the rear of the warehouse, but as this photograph appears, the witness indicated that he jumped from one of three or four small windows that can clearly be seen on this photograph in the centre of the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Witness, can you describe to the Judges what you could see around you at this point, if anything at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: When I jumped from the window and fell to the ground, I just heard a voice from the corn field. I didn't know that there were guards around, and that there were guards. If I had known, I wouldn't have dared jump. I wouldn't have had the courage, because they would have killed me. So when I jumped and fell to the ground, I just heard a voice saying, "There's one that just jumped." And then when I fell to the ground, I saw in front of me, to my right, there were two dead men lying on the ground. Most probably, they had also tried to save their lives and escape and, unfortunately, they failed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that you heard a voice, let me get this right, coming from the corn field. Can you indicate to the Judges on this photograph, the corn field that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes, I can [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let the record show that the witness is identifying on Prosecutor's Exhibit 8/9 that the piece of ground covered in snow which is immediately in front of the building and which has some plants growing on it, corn, old corn growing on it is the corn field to which the witness is referring.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, it was summertime when you were there, it was July. Was the corn higher than is shown in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes, of course it was much higher. And it was still green, it hadn't ripened yet, but it was very high. So if I were to stand up straight, though I didn't stand up straight, if I were to stand up straight, it would be higher than me, the maize.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you said today that you saw that there were two dead men lying on the ground and that they had tried to save their lives, and you stated unfortunately, they failed. Can you recall what happened to you next?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes, of course I remember. When I heard this voice from the maize, "There's one that's just jumped out," immediately a man headed towards me through the maize. And the searchlights went on, and the person who passed by me, I could feel. I wasn't looking at him. I was facing the wall from which I had just jumped, the window, rather. He was carrying this searchlight which had been switched on and, of course, he carried a rifle, but I didn't see that. But I could feel the flash of the light against the wall. And this Serb soldier was approaching me. I knew that was my end. I didn't try to run, though I could have tried, but I didn't want to. I waited for him to kill me. So that if I had tried to run, he would have certainly killed me. There were several of them. I waited for him to kill me. He approached two metres from me and he shot a single bullet at me, so that he hit me in the back, my right shoulder blade. It was an entry and exit wound. I kept quiet; I didn't speak or say anything. He asked me, "Do you want more?" I remained silent, without uttering a sound, to try and persuade him that I was dead. I pretended to be dead, and of course I succeeded, he really thought I was dead, but luckily I was alive. Then he cried out that his clip had fallen out, so that a second man approached him and they found the clip. And they left me, they went back into the maize. After that I continued to hear bursts of fire and shots being fired at people in the warehouse where I was, I heard them killing people there, so that I remained there all night, until morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness, if you could just pause there for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 8/9, which is the one I think that was on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you could indicate to the Judges on this photograph where you lay that night, approximately.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Here [indicates]. Here [indicates], perhaps half a metre from the wall, here [indicates], on the grass. To my left was the maize field. My head was turned towards the river, or rather towards Kladanj, and my legs towards Bratunac, shall I put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That's very clear, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let the record show that the witness has indicated, on Prosecutor's Exhibit 8/9, that he was lying on some grass between the factory building and the cornfield, with his head facing towards the left-hand side of the photograph and his legs to the right-hand side of the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you said that you stayed there all night. Did anybody come and check your body during the night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: No, no one came.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges what you recall from the next day, from the next morning, what happened to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: When it dawned?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: When it dawned, Witness, yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: I was still lying there. I didn't dare move because I was thinking and I was afraid that someone might come to check whether I was still on that spot or whether I had escaped. So when the sun rose, I heard yells and a noise. People were yelling and asking whether anyone inside was left alive, in the warehouse. Of course there were some people who were alive. So they promised them, I heard a voice saying, the Bosnian Serbs promising and saying that the Red Cross had come and that the first aid people had come to take them to the hospital to treat them. And whoever could walk and crawl out of the warehouse, they came out. I didn't see them coming out. I didn't see them taking them out. And probably they sat down there somewhere; I don't know because I couldn't see it. And then this one man, of course I assume it was the leader who was giving the orders, who was in command, he ordered them to sing songs, Serb songs, Chetnik songs, rather. As far as I could hear, I remember well that they sang the song "From Topolje to Ravne Gora, there are all our guards of General Draza," and many other songs that I had remembered but I've forgotten in the meantime. After that, they went on singing for about half an hour or an hour, I'm not sure, then I heard bursts of fire. The fire went on for some time, I don't know for how long, a certain amount of time. They killed those wounded, and later I didn't hear anything anymore, I never heard them singing those songs. But they were dragging them inside, into the warehouse. After that I heard a voice, one of those Bosnian Serbs said, "There are some dead around the building. They need to be collected." So I was even more afraid there. I panicked because I thought they would collect me and they would see I was alive and then they would kill me. Then another one said, "Well, they are not a problem. We'll collect them later. Let's deal with those who are inside." Then they were shooting them in their heads. I heard them inside, they were saying something like, "I think this one is still alive. Shoot him in the head," and then you would hear a bullet, one, two, or several, shooting at those they thought were still alive. After that I heard a loud noise inside, in the hangar. The excavator, the dredger, was collecting the dead, and in my view they were probably loading them onto a truck and driving them to graves. I could not see the direction they took. So that I still remained in the same spot, lying there. After a while I heard somebody walking through the maize field toward me. It was a Bosnian Serb soldier. I realised immediately that it was the soldier who had shot me the previous night. He came to a metre from me, perhaps. Judging by the sound, he stopped very close to me. I was stinking like a corpse, covered in blood. There were flies all over me. As I said, the sun was high and it was hot. And when he approached me, the flies flew off me, they flew away. And he was there for maybe half a minute or a minute; I don't know exactly, anyway, very briefly. So he didn't say anything, he didn't touch me, he just broke off a leaf from the maize plant and he sounded as if he had a cold, he was sniffing. And then he went back again through the maize field. While he was approaching me, I held my breath so that he couldn't notice that I was breathing, so in that way I managed to make him believe that I was dead. When he left, no other person came close. After that I raised my head a little and I looked in front of me. I was all stiff because I didn't dare budge all night. Then I stretched my arms and legs a little, and I saw that everything was all right, that I could walk, it wasn't too painful. Then I turned to look around behind me, and I saw the hangar behind me and I saw Bosnian Serbs entering, entering the other hangar. On that hangar they were entering, I saw some red letters but I don't remember what was written on that hangar. The letters were written in a straight line, vertically, in red.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness, if you could wait there for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 116.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you and I viewed a video yesterday afternoon, which I think is Prosecutor's Exhibit 8/9.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: It's a video that's in evidence. I'll give the Court a number in a moment. It's actually Prosecutor's Exhibit 8/13, the video that Your Honours saw of the Kravica warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: In fact, you noticed on this video that the lettering that you saw on the building is -- if the photograph could be put centrally. Could you point to the lettering, the vertical lettering, that you saw when you got up on that day, in July, on the other building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes, of course I'll show it. They are these letters [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let the record show that the witness is indicating, on Prosecutor's Exhibit 116, a series of seven letters that are set vertically on a white building, a part of the factory complex in Kravica, and they are located just above and to the right of the door, which is just off centre in the photograph. If the witness could then be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 8/2.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you could just indicate on this photograph the building on which those letters were written from which you saw Bosnian Serb soldiers entering.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Of course I'll show you. It's this building here [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let the record show that the witness is indicating, on Prosecutor's Exhibit 8/2, to the part of the factory complex, the warehouse building, which is furthest to the left. It's above the road and it's the building furthest to the left, and it's perpendicular to the road that runs from the left to the right of the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, after you'd got up, after you'd seen this lettering, what did you do next?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: I sort of stretched out a little while I was still lying down.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Sorry, Witness, it's just we need that photograph again, and rather than have the usher bring it back.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: It's Exhibit 8/2. You can just leave that Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you, Witness, you said that you stretched out a little. You were still lying down. What happened to you next?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes. As I was saying, I stretched my legs and arms. I looked to the left through the maize. I saw them entering again, Bosnian Serbs. It was a little way away from me. They were entering the lower hangar and to my left. I'll show it to you on the picture [indicates]. They were entering this hangar. This one.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you could just wait there, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: By this hangar, next to this hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let the record show that the witness is indicating on Prosecutor's Exhibit 8/2 the white rectangular building which is furthest in the background of the photograph and has a striped effected front, the front of the building has -- appears to have black and white stripes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Please continue, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: In the course of the night, in this building, I will show you now [indicates], in this building, I heard to my left, I think it was in this building, that there must have been cows screaming, something was squealing like pigs. I don't know what it was. To me, it sounded like cows. There were some cries anyway and screams. And, as I have just said, I saw those Bosnian Serbs, two or three of them I saw. Once when I had decided to run from the place I was lying, I saw them entering this hangar to my left. And then, I crawled to the left through the maize for a distance of some two or three metres, maybe more. So I entered a line of the maize and I headed -- if I'm looking at the picture, as I am now, towards the river. I'll show you now. And I crawled as far as the river. From here to the right [indicates]. I reached this corner here [indicates]. I looked to the right to make sure there were no Bosnian Serbs to see me there. And while I was crawling through the maize, I was going very slowly so that no one would notice any movement. I saw two or three bodies here [indicates]. The soil was clay near the river, and the maize couldn't grow from the clay soil, it was very small, very short, maybe only half a metre from the ground, maybe even smaller. And I saw three Muslim men dead there. One of them had a shot wound in his head.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness, if you could just indicate again, without speaking, the route that you took from behind the warehouse, and I'll describe it so that it's on our transcript. So if you can just indicate, with the pointer, the route that you took from behind the warehouse?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: What do you mean? While I was crawling or while we were on the bus?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: While you were crawling.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: I see. I'll show you. This is where I was [indicates], and this is the distance that I covered crawling to my right side in the direction of the river, if you're looking at the picture the way I am now. So this is the way I took, and this is the spot where I actually entered [indicates] the brook, the creek. I stayed five minutes -- for about five minutes there. I drank some water. I washed myself a little. And I saw another dead body here [indicates] who also had a gunshot wound in his head. It must have been a Muslim who had tried to save his life, but didn't manage to. So I crossed the river --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness, if you could wait.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let the record show that the route that the witness took on Prosecutor's Exhibit 8/2 is a route that he indicated immediately behind the main factory building which is in the centre of the photograph, immediately behind that building to its extreme right end, and then up diagonally into an area that appears to have bushes and trees where he indicated there was a brook.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you said that you went into a brook where you washed yourself and you drank some water. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes, of course I recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How long did you spend in that small river?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: About five minutes, at least I think it was five. I didn't have a watch.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And after you left that little brook, where did you go after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: I'll show you on the picture. At this corner here [indicates], this is where I drank some water, where I washed myself at the brook. So I moved maybe five or ten metres upwards and then I turned back. And then I turned towards the warehouse and I could still hear the sound of the excavator collecting dead bodies from the warehouse. I was looking for a bottle or a container of some kind so that I could take some water for me for later on to refresh myself, but I couldn't find anything. So I crossed the brook and I entered another cornfield. This is the other cornfield [indicates]. And I walked through the cornfield, through one line of the corns, and I reached a small path which cannot be seen on the picture, and this is where I entered the woods. Again, I felt very weak. I was about to faint. And this is where I found an empty can. I continued for about 20 to 30 metres along that path and I came up to a brook again.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the record could just show that the route that the witness indicated was a cornfield in the top right-hand corner of the photograph and that he left through the cornfield and then followed a path which is not shown on this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness, you said you found an empty can and you continued for 20 to 30 metres along a path and you came to a brook again. Now, I know from you and I having spoken that you had quite a difficult journey after this, but I want to cut matters short. I think I'm right in saying that you eventually found yourself in the town of Zepa on, I think, the 26th of July of 1995; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what date it was. I know only that I was in Zepa, that's true. But it was before the fall of Zepa at any rate.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you know when Zepa fell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: I don't know, because I had left before the town fell, and the Bosnian Serbs had already entered the area. Maybe it was two, three, four, maybe five days later, and I stayed a while in the hospital in Zepa. So when we went down to Zepa, the 12 of us who were wounded, we decided to join a convoy with the civilian population; women, children, and elderly people towards Kladanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: While you were in Zepa, were you registered by the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes. When I came to Zepa, together with a colleague of mine, a friend of mine whose name was Senad. I forgot his last name. He's from Voljavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I want to show you your Red Cross certificate which is Exhibit 118. Mr. Usher don't put this on the ELMO because it has the witness' name on it, but if copies of it could be given to the witness and Judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness, don't read anything from this certificate, but can you just confirm that this is the Red Cross certificate confirming that you were originally registered in Zepa and then subsequently visited at the Rogatica military camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I was registered together with everybody else. There were, I believe, 12 of us who had been wounded. We entered the UN Compound where the Ukranian Battalion was stationed, and this is where the Red Cross people came and registered us. The Bosnian Serbs, the military, had already entered the town of Zepa, and they were walking around the area. They were together there while the evacuation of civilians was taking place towards Kladanj. Then French doctors came and examined us together with a Serb doctor. This doctor examined me as well, and then they were selecting wounded people. They wouldn't let them do it. They let some of them go. There were quite a few elderly people there; people who could not walk, could not move, and they were evacuated by the French military in their APCs. Some of the wounded were put on buses, but the 12 of us who remained, they didn't let us go --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cayley, I'm sorry to interrupt you at this point because the text has already disappeared from the screen. The exhibit that we saw was 5/18 and the transcript on page 91 which is no longer here stated 6/18. I would just like to make sure that it was 5/18.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I know that after the proceedings, the stenographers actually go through the recorded -- the record and actually correct all of these numbers. So it will be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then, because I didn't say 5/18 or 6/18. I said -- well, if a correction is going to be made, then it will be corrected, because I wanted to say that it was not Exhibit 1/18, yes, but the exhibit number 5/18. I'm sorry, I see 5/18 once again. As far as I can see, it's 5/18 and I wanted to say 118. That is 118. I'm sorry. It's my mistake. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, you have success at the end. You have 118 on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness, in summary, and if you could just answer yes or no, the Defence may have some more detailed questions than this, but am I right in saying that you were promised that you would be taken to free territory and, in fact, you found yourself in the Bosnian Serb prison camp at Rogatica. That's where the Bosnian Serbs actually took you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And I think you stayed in that camp until the 15th of January, 1996, and you were then taken to Kula prison and exchanged at Sarajevo airport on the 19th of January of 1996; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If I could just briefly show you Prosecutor's Exhibit 117, which, again, Mr. Usher, is a document that's not to go on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: (redacted). I'm not going to go through them all, but if you could just confirm that these are your medical records which you provided to the Office of the Prosecutor a number of years ago, I think two years ago. Are these your medical records?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes, these are my medical records.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: (redacted).

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, I know you suffered some trauma as a result of these events, and that's shown in your medical records. How do you feel now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: I don't feel very well. That's all I can tell you. But all in all it's okay. I cannot complain.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you still have any night-time recollection of the events at Kravica? Do you still have dreams or nightmares about these events?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes, of course I do. I have dreams. I wake up in the middle of the night and I shiver. I become anxious, I start trembling, and everything comes back to my mind, my journey from Srebrenica to Tuzla. Everything sort of passes through me once again and it makes me fearful again. It's difficult to describe how I feel.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness, thank you very much, indeed, for your patience. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I can now offer the witness for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Cayley. I think we should have a break now because one member of the Chamber has an urgent obligation. I don't know how much time you will need, Mr. Petrusic, for your cross-examination. Could you tell us that now?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, of course it will depend on the answers given by the witness, but we hope to finish before the end of the day. However, this is not a 100 per cent reliable estimate, but we will do our best to complete the cross-examination today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But in any case we have to have a break. We will have a 15-minute break, and after that we will continue. Thank you very much, Mr. Petrusic. A 15-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you can see, Judge Fouad Riad was unable to rejoin us, and in line with Rule 15 bis we're going to continue with the testimony of this witness. Mr. Petrusic, you have the floor. Witness, you are now going to answer questions put to you by Counsel Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness K.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: At the very beginning, I should like to ask you, where did you start out from in the direction of Jaglici, on the 11th of July, I think it was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: We headed towards Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: But where from? You yourself.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: From Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: A group of able-bodied men rallied in Jaglici, did they not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So could you please wait a couple of seconds after my question, since we speak the same language, for the benefit of the interpreters. Just three seconds or so. So this group went on along which road?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: I'm afraid I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: When you got together in Jaglici, you headed towards which position, along which path, which route?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: We headed towards Tuzla, through the woods.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You said in the course of your testimony today that you were not armed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: During the examination-in-chief, you said that you were unarmed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: When? Where?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: I mean Jaglici and on from there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes. The majority were not armed, of the men, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In your statement to the Agency for Investigation and Documentation, AID, on the 16th of February, 1996, you said, on page 2 --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I ask the usher for his assistance, please. Could the statement be given to the Chamber, the Prosecution, and the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It will be Exhibit D14.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So on page 2, the first sentence: "After a short lull, the Chetniks opened fire at us again, demanding that we surrender our weapons, which we did not agree to."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Therefore, this was an armed group.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: No, they didn't see that. But they called on all of us, whoever had any weapons, to surrender them, or if they had any, to surrender them. They thought that we were all armed and we were not. Very few men had rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Witness K, you said that you didn't agree to surrender your weapons, so my question is: Was yours an armed group of men or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: I don't understand. Do you mean a small group or all the men who were heading towards Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: The group that you were in.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: The group I was in? They called on all of us to surrender, anyone who had any weapons. All men who were armed were called on by them to throw down their weapons, or to surrender. Of course, when the surrender occurred, no one reached them with their weapons on them. They wouldn't give themselves up armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You're talking about the group you were in, and you said that you didn't accept their offer, shall we call it that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Therefore, that group did have weapons.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: We did, but we didn't surrender together with our weapons. The moment that I decided to go and surrender, together with a group of men, none of us had any weapons because people threw away their weapons in the woods. They didn't dare surrender with their weapons on them, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So let us make this quite clear. The moment that you were called upon, did you and your group have weapons on you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: The moment they called on us, I did not have a weapon just then.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So you are claiming that the statement you made to AID is not correct.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Regarding this part that we're referring to.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: I don't understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Objection. Your Honour, I think it should actually be made very clear what the witness said in his statement, and I think there is a slight degree of misrepresentation that is taking place by Mr. Petrusic. The witness did not state in his statement that he refused to do anything, and Mr. Petrusic has actually offered it to the witness in that fashion, "You refused to lay down your arms." If I read from the English version, it states: "After a short silence, the Chetniks opened fire on us again, demanding that we surrender our weapons to them, which we refused to do." The witness has been asked on a number of occasions whether or not there were armed persons in the column. He's acknowledged that. He said that there were a number of people that were armed in the column. Mr. Petrusic is asking essentially the same question over and over again, to which he's getting the same response. So I think he should be asked to move on with his cross-examination, and I think that the witness has satisfactorily answered the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petrusic, what is your response? What is your reaction to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My response, Mr. President, is that I am not misrepresenting what the witness said, I'm just asking him whether what he said was correct or not. Maybe we can put the question in that way. The sentence that has been quoted from his statement, does it reflect the real state of affairs at that point in time, on the 11th of July, and at that spot where he was?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Petrusic, but I think that the witness has already explained, in a way. But if the witness has answered, maybe you should move forward and go on to another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness K.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to ask the usher to be kind enough to put on the ELMO Prosecutor's Exhibit 8/4. Could you please move it to the right a little, the photograph to the right, to the right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In relation to the left part of the photograph, where we see these two pillars, below the sign saying "Kravica", can the witness tell us where the buses stopped?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes, I'll show you on the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: The front part of the bus, where did it stop?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Here [indicates], further to the left, off the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So for the record, it can be noted that it is to the left of the area shown on the photograph, underneath the first window.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You disembarked from the bus, and can you then explain where you went to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: On the photograph? You want me to show you on the photograph?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Describe it, and then we'll see for the record.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: I got off the bus. I entered the first entrance there. Just in front of this pillar where it says "Kravica". To the left of the first pillar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did you pass in front of the bus?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: What do you mean in front? How?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: The bus, the bus was at a standstill. It was stopped. You got off the bus. Did you have to pass in front of the bus, the driver's side?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I passed around the front of the bus, and we were quickly pushed into the warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: This part of the warehouse which has these two supporting pillars, is it partitioned in relation to the left closed part of the warehouse?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: What do you mean left, which side?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: On the left of the photograph. You see the part of the warehouse which is closed in.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: I can't see it being closed in. I can only see the outside wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In relation to the outside wall that you can see, and in relation to the front part with the two supporting pillars, is there any partition between these two premises?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Between the two pillars? I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Between the open part of the warehouse and the part where we can only see the outside wall that is walled in; is there a partition there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And is there a door on that partitioning partition?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: I didn't see it. There was some kind of a fence, like a fence that was broken or something, as far as I could see.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did that go the whole length of the building? That fence, did it go along the whole breadth of the building, rather?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: I didn't notice that. I don't know. I was unable to register whether it did or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us how long, how high that fence was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: How could I know? I didn't measure it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did it look like a door?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: No, it was a fence, like any fence. Like this external fence that is shown on the photograph, rather like that, something like that. Now how high it was, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Were you placed behind that fence to the left?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: I mean the part of the building that we only see the outside wall of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes, to the left. When we went inside and sat down, I was looking in front. To my right was the entrance where I went through, and in front of me was the fence and the wall, the partition, some kind of a partition.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Perhaps it will be easier if we look at Exhibit 8/9.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So as not to waste time, Mr. President, I can give the usher a copy myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Witness K, in relation to these two windows through which we can see the panorama behind the warehouse, were you in this right-hand wing of this warehouse?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes, I'll show it to you [indicates]. In this area, in this part [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Does this include the part where you encircled two open windows, those that you can see through?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Was your whole group in that part of the building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: What do you mean the "whole group"?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: All of you who came from Lolici. And according to your estimate, there were 1.000 to 1.500. Were they all accommodated there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: All the people who came in the buses, as far as I saw, were unloaded and placed in those hangars. When I entered the warehouse, I didn't see outside whether others may have, perhaps, been taken to another warehouse because we were very much afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You said that there was a fence, Witness K?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Were you all on one side of that fence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: All of us who were there with me, yes, who were with me. As far as I was able to see, we were all there on one side of the fence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Let me -- delete that, please. I know that you were fearful, that you probably didn't notice many details, but could you roughly tell us the size of the premise that you were in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Roughly, let me try. It would be, perhaps, the length of the warehouse where I was, it seemed to me to be maybe about 30 metres long, 40, maybe less. That's how it looked to me. And the width was maybe 15 metres, I don't know, maybe less, maybe more. That is very roughly my estimation. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: These two young men who were taken out of the warehouse allegedly to assist in collecting the wounded, did they come back to the warehouse?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did you ask them where they went, in fact?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: No, it never occurred to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Not one of those from your group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did they, themselves, say anything?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: No, we just kept quiet to see what was going to happen. We were all in a panic and great fear.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Were there any injuries on them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Witness K, as you said, you were crammed into that warehouse very close to one another so that, as you put it, you couldn't move left or right an inch?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Not quite like that. You misunderstood me, sir. It's not true that we really couldn't budge. But I said, and I am saying, that we were crammed full so if you would try to get up and go out, you couldn't stand on the ground, on the concrete. You'd have to lean against someone else for a person to try and get -- walk out, if somebody wanted to get out.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: It was obviously very crowded there, but when the Serb soldiers entered and started shooting, you said that you threw yourself on the ground?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to me where did you throw yourself to in view of the fact that you were so crowded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: I threw myself on the ground. The Serb soldier who opened fire lay on -- I lay on my stomach, and I remained lying like that on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So when the soldier opened fire. So in view of the fact that it was so crowded, as you said a moment ago, now, suddenly, you have enough space to throw yourself face down on the ground?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Let me explain in greater detail, sir. I see that it is not clear to you, so I want to make sure you understand me properly. The Serb soldier, when he opened fire, after that, a couple of others, maybe five or six of them, I don't know how many, I don't know exactly. When they opened fire, there was panic, and people jumped to their feet, one on top of another. We saw what was happening and they were going to kill all of us. So when the people jumped up off the ground, in view of the terrible fear that was widespread, I threw myself on the ground, though there wasn't too much space, but I sort of stuck to the ground without getting up. And after that, people started falling on top of me; dead, wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Witness K, before you climbed the container to get to the window and jump out, did you cross this fence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: No, I didn't cross the fence. The container was below the window to my left or, rather, as we can see on the photograph. It was to the left of me. So I went diagonally towards the window and towards that container. I climbed on the container so that I stepped on to the window sill and then I jumped out. I fell to the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: How long did you remain beneath this window, below the window?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: For the whole night.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And after that, as you have already explained, you went to the creek, to the small river, rivulet. And there were Serb soldiers everywhere around you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: What do you mean "everywhere"?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Well, in the immediate vicinity, in relation to this small river.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Of course I didn't know that they were there. If I had known that they were there, that they had surrounded the warehouse, I wouldn't have dared jump out because they would have killed me. I thought they weren't there. I thought that only those outside the entrance of the hangar were there next to the road. When I jumped out and fell to the ground, I heard a voice from the maize saying, "There's one jumping out," and then I realised that there were guards there, Serb army guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: The machine that you describe as a dredger or excavator which was collecting the bodies, you didn't see it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And in which part of the warehouse was this machine?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: You mean -- I didn't see it, but I heard the noise. This was in the same direction that I jumped.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In relation to this photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Well, that was my impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Could you show us on this photograph on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes, I can. You want me to show you where this excavator was? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Exactly.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Here [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the record, the witness is showing the back part of the warehouse, viewed from the direction of Bratunac, Kravica. Yes, Bratunac, Kravica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petrusic, you mean the right part of the photograph, right-hand side of the photograph?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I was trying to describe the direction of the road, but I quite agree with you that it is the right-hand side of the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: After that you reached Zepa.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: On the 26th of July.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date when I arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Immediately after your arrival in Zepa, did representatives of the International Red Cross give you an ID card?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: No, not straight away. I was in hospital for four or five days.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You were promised evacuation.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes, we were promised that by the Bosnian Serbs, and the Red Cross made this promise.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And then you went to prison in Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: No. Together with 12 wounded and some elderly men and women and children from Zepa, we headed towards Kladanj. We had a rest at Boksanica. There was the Ukrainian checkpoint. Night fell while we were there. And I heard there that Ratko Mladic had come, General of the Bosnian Serb army, with a helicopter. I saw the helicopter. And the commander of Rogatica came with an escort, asking where we came from, but they didn't hurt anyone. After that we continued towards Kladanj. I don't know the places but I heard them mention the name Luka. We got close to Kladanj and then the army of Republika Srpska stopped the buses. Of course, they had lists from the Red Cross that had registered us, they had listed all of us and the wounded, and they read out from the lists and ordered us to get off and to board other buses. There were quite a number of old men too there; they probably needed them for labour, as this proved to be later. And then they drove us towards Rogatica, the camp there. That's where we ended up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petrusic, excuse me for interrupting you, but I would like to know whether you intend to finish today or whether we should leave the cross-examination for tomorrow. Let's try and finish with the witness so as not to make him come tomorrow. But I would like to know whether you need a lot more time or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will bear in mind your suggestion, Mr. President. I'm almost done. A couple of minutes more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, Mr. Petrusic, would you make your questions precise and concrete? Then the witness will answer in a similar fashion. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Witness K, in your statement given to an investigator of this Tribunal, on the 26th of November, 1998, you stated that you had been taken off the bus because you had a pair of military trousers on.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: That I was taken off the bus?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: "I assume that I had been taken off the bus and that I was not evacuated because I was wearing military trousers."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Which location do you have in mind? Where?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: I'm reading from your statement, the statement that you gave on the 26th of November, 1998.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Sir, I asked you about the location where I was taken off, where I was separated, whether it was in Zepa or at Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: If we disregard the exact location, because you're not referring to it in your statement, I should like to know whether this is, indeed, what you stated.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: While I was in hospital in Zepa, while I was wounded, I found a pair of multicoloured trousers of Russian make, and that was the only clothing that I could get hold of. It was the bottom part of the clothing. I couldn't walk around naked. I also had a pair of cowboy boots on. This is what I had found somewhere in the forest after I had fled the execution site in Kravica. Because I was barefoot, I had to throw away my shoes at one point, and then in one discarded backpack, I found a pair of cowboy boots, and this is how I reached Zepa, wearing those boots.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have no further questions. Witness K, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Petrusic. Do you have any further questions, Mr. Cayley? No. Thank you. Judge Wald.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Just a very few questions, Witness K. You say you were a member of the Bosnian army at the time that you joined the column moving towards Tuzla. Were all the men in that column members of the Bosnian army, and if not, what proportion would you say were not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: I couldn't give you the exact number. Of course, I was a member of the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Would you say the majority of people in the column were members of the Bosnian army or the majority were not and were just civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: The majority were civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. My second question is: Why did you surrender? I mean, what were the circumstances when you had started on the march that made you and your fellow marchers surrender?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Bosnian Serbs had encircled us from all sides. I had already spent one night there, and when it dawned, we reached a meadow just above Konjevic Polje -- I don't know the name of the place but it was near the wood -- and I continued like that for about 100 metres, in the direction of the asphalt road, and this is where I found a large group of people who were unarmed, had no weapons. They were simply standing there. They were confused; they didn't know where to go, what to do, whether to surrender or not. And the Bosnian Serb army had completely surrounded us, we had no where to go, and this is how we decided to surrender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. At the point that you escaped from the Kravica warehouse by jumping out of the window, you told us that you didn't know that there were soldiers on the outside or you might not have jumped. But were there soldiers guarding the prisoners on the inside of the warehouse, and if so, roughly how many?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes, occasionally they would enter the warehouse. Five or six of them would always be inside. Sometimes only three would remain; sometimes there would be five of them. They would watch us, walk around, and then leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: How, then, do you think you were able to get over to the container, get on top of the container and jump out without one of them seeing you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Well, they were inside before they opened fire on us. This was before. But after that, when everything became quiet and the smoke dispersed, then one by one they would enter and throw in hand grenades, or they would finish off those who had remained alive, wounded. So when they thought that everybody had been killed, there was a longer lull in shooting, and at that point I decided to jump through the window to save myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. My last question is: When you were in Zepa, you mentioned that they were beginning to evacuate, or they were evacuating not only the wounded but some women and children and others. Were you in a position to see some of that evacuation taking place? I mean, were you in a position so that you saw some of the civilians in Zepa being evacuated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes, of course, I was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So if that's right, are you able to tell us whether or not, in that evacuation, the men were separated from the women and children, and the women and children were put on vehicles and evacuated but the men were not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: I didn't see men being separated. The able-bodied men had gone to the mountain, those who had weapons, and only civilians remained together with us, the wounded. The wounded were separated and taken to the Ukrainian Battalion compound. But I could observe the evacuation of people from Zepa, and they included women, children, and the elderly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: But there was no formal process that you observed of separating the men out from the women and children for evacuation, of those that were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: No, I didn't observe that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: And the Red Cross was observing the evacuation; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Witness K.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cayley and Mr. Petrusic, what is the status of our exhibits? I can see that there are several of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. If I could apply for admission into evidence of the following: The first exhibit is Prosecutor's Exhibit 8A/2, which is a map which the witness used to demonstrate to the Judges the route that he took. Exhibit 118, which is the witness' registration by the Red Cross. That certificate should remain under seal because it has the witness' name and date of birth upon it. The next exhibit is Exhibit 119, which is a sketch which the witness produced when he was originally interviewed by the OTP. That document should remain under seal because it has upon it the signature of the witness and his name. There's also 119 bis, which is a public document, which is the redacted version. It has the signature and name of the witness removed. Exhibit 117, which are the medical records of the witness concerning the injuries he suffered at Kravica, that document should remain under seal because it has identifying features. And then the last exhibit is Exhibit 116, which is the still taken from a video, showing letters in a perpendicular fashion on one of the factory buildings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Petrusic, any objections as regards the exhibits tendered under seal?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, we do not object to the exhibits tendered by the Prosecutor. We would also like to tender D14 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cayley, any objection to this one, D14? No. Thank you very much. Therefore, Exhibit D14, Prosecutor's 8A/2, 118, 119, and 117 will be admitted into evidence, including two exhibits admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. These exhibits have been admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, Mr. Dubuisson. Mr. Cayley, any remarks?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: It's my fault, actually, Mr. President, because I gave you the exhibits out of order. There's also Exhibit 116, which I actually mentioned last on the list but which you didn't mention when you were admitting these exhibits into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Maybe you didn't get the interpretation, but I remember mentioning it. Exhibit 116, is that the one? Yes. Very well, then. Thank you very much, Mr. Cayley. Before we adjourn for the day, I should like to tell the parties that we would like to have a short Status Conference on the 13th of this month, this week therefore. We will have to finish the session at ten minutes past two and we will try to have a 20-minute-long Status Conference. The reason for this Status Conference is that I should like to see where we are in relation to the plan that was established at the beginning, that is, how can we save even more time and speed up things a little bit. So I should like to hear the Prosecutor as regards the possibility of finishing his case, the Prosecution case, before the summer recess, and also I should like to hear the Defence and the plans as regarding their case, because we have to bear in mind the schedule. We will after that try to set up a calendar, after this Status Conference, taking into account all the possibilities that remain open. So this was all that I wanted to tell you for the time being. I should also like to address the witness before he leaves. Witness K, you have finished your testimony before the International Criminal Tribunal. Thank you very much for coming to testify here. We do hope that you will have a long life and that you will be able to change your opinion, what you mentioned here. You said that you had seen a number of horror films and that which you experienced was much worse. We do agree with you, but we also hope that you will be able to find courage to change that perspective in life. Thank you. So tomorrow at 9.30 we will gather here again. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
